title: Tissue-Anchored vs. Circulating Engineered Enzyme Constructs for Immunometabolic Resolution of Psoriasis
text:
We have engineered innovative fusion protein enzyme constructs in tissue-anchored and
circulating forms as therapeutics to shut down Th17-driven inflammation through metabolic
reprogramming. We are applying these to the inflammatory autoimmune disease psoriasis, which
is in need of new clinical options.

title: Molecular determinants of voltage-gated ion channels' localization and function
text:
Voltage-gated ion channels are essential for the proper function of multiple cells and tissues. The proposed
research aims to fill key gaps in our understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating their transport,
organization and activity. This work will elucidate conserved pathways that could inform novel therapeutic targets
for treatment of illnesses including cancer, neurological and muscular disorders.

title: Precision Deaminases to Expand the Scope of Diseases Amenable to CRISPR-mediated Correction
text:
Most genetic variants associated with disease are single point mutations which are potentially correctable via
systems that exchange a single DNA base (base editors). However, the capacity of this approach is limited by
editing promiscuity at neighboring bases which constrains target selection to a narrow range of mutations where
nearby off-target edits would not negate the effect of the edit or induce additional pathogenic mutations. This
proposal addresses an unmet clinical need for the advent of precision editors using a two-pronged approach that
extends existing technology and creates an entirely new kind of editing enzyme with intrinsic properties that
prevent off-target edits.

title: Coordinated mental simulation in the hippocampus and primary visual cortex during active behavior
text:
The brain can travel in space and time to generate representations that do not refer to the current experience
(“mental simulations”), a remarkable capability supported by distributed neural circuits in the mammalian brain
including the hippocampus and primary visual cortex. To address our limited understanding of the neural
mechanism underlying mental simulations, this proposal will leverage cutting-edge experimental and
computational tools to decode a common cognitive variable from the hippocampus and primary visual cortex
and examine the factors that influence their remarkable coordination. This work will enhance our knowledge of
how the cognitive brain influences the sensory brain and provide insights into psychiatric disorders that affect
visual perception, such as schizophrenia.

title: Ablating Liver Metastases with SBRT to Enhance Immune Checkpoint Blockade in Melanoma
text:
Rational combinatorial approaches are urgently needed to enhance immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy in
patients with liver metastases. We have discovered that liver metastases siphon and delete tumor-specific T
cells to cause systemic immunotherapy resistance, and moreover that ablative liver-directed radiotherapy can
restore immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy. Herein we propose to evaluate mechanisms of immunotherapy
resistance in melanoma patients and preclinical melanoma models with liver metastases as well as
mechanistically define how liver SBRT overcomes immunotherapy resistance.

title: Tools to enable brain wide chronic electrophysiology in freely moving rodents
text:
Tools to enable brain wide chronic electrophysiology in freely moving
rodents
The availability of 1536 channels electrophysiology probes opens the gateway to brain wide
recording in freely moving animals. To make the capability practical, a variety of engineering
developments will be addressed: Robotic assisted surgery to make multiprobe implants faster
and more reliable, enhanced data acquisition software to manage the very large data sets, and
enhanced analysis software to create reliable outcomes without manual curation. These will be
exercised with a navigation task in mice and rats to optimize discovery of brain wide navigation
neural activity.

title: Systems Metabolic Approach for Multi-scale Pancreatic Cancer Phenotyping
text:
PROJECTIVE NARRATIVE
Pancreatic cancer is an aggressive, devastating malignancy with despondent morbidity and mortality. While
there have been advancements in clinical imaging, histology, and cellular/molecular profiling, these
advancements have occurred largely independent of one another, thus there is a need to integrate these to
provide a more causal understanding of how clinical imaging phenotypes relate to pancreatic adenocarcinoma
subtypes from more to less aggressive subtypes, and in the process establish “molecular omic-type to clinical
phenotype” relationship in order to find new strategies to diagnosis and treat the disease. The work in this
proposal will use cutting-edge cellular and tissue measurements of the microenvironment of pancreatic
adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with computational systems biology (using integrated transcription, signaling, and
metabolic networks), focusing on the of glycolytic and inflammatory characteristics of tumors in relation to
specific histological tumor characteristics, in order to 1) develop a non-invasive imaging test (i.e. anatomical
and metabolic imaging through PET/CT) to identify PDAC phenotypes that 2) lead to new potential cellular
targets for treatment in the future.

title: Perinatal human cerebellum development: high-resolution in-vivo and ex-vivo imaging
text:
Perinatal cerebellar injury is widely associated with developmental delays in motor, language, cognition, and
social behaviors. However, the underlying biological processes -- causing functional disorders -- have not yet
been fully understood. This study proposes to establish high-resolution structure and connectivity maps of the
developing cerebellum using both in vivo and ex vivo imaging during the first year of life and to characterize
healthy neurodevelopment and developmental disorders under perinatal cerebellar injury in large cohorts. Our
study offers a viable tool for both characterizing early cerebellar development and identifying biomarkers to
predict the developmental outcomes in perinatal cerebellar injury.

title: GEMRA: Geriatric Emergency Medicine Risk Prediction Model for Return VisitAdmissions
text:
In older adults, emergency department (ED) return visits resulting in a hospital admission (RVA) have
dramatically higher morbidity and mortality than patients admitted on their initial ED visit. We propose to develop
an automated ED screening tool to identify older adults at risk of RVA within 72 hours following an initial ED visit,
using machine learning to accurately predict this multifactorial event. Findings from this research will improve
the ability of ED clinicians to identify this vulnerable population for subsequent risk-mitigating interventions.

title: Cardiovascular risk from comprehensive evaluation of the CT calcium score exam
text:
We will create artificial intelligence methods for quantitative assessment of heart disease using a fast, inexpen-
sive computed tomography (CT) imaging method. With success, our research will lead to improved evaluation
of heart disease, paving the way for personalized treatments. It will also enable many research studies on oth-
er risk factors such as diabetes.

title: Leveraging routinely collected health data to improve understanding of language development in children identified as late talkers
text:
The purpose of the renewal of the Duke Autism Center of Excellence is to apply cutting-edge, translational digital
health and computational methods to develop more effective tools for early autism screening and for objectively
monitoring changes in children’s behavior, and to discover novel, brain-based biomarkers that can be used for
stratification and to assess target engagement in clinical trials with young autistic children. Our long-term vision
is to transform how clinical care is delivered by providing innovative solutions that address long-standing barriers
in access to care and enhance our ability to evaluate interventions that will improve quality of life of autistic
children and their families.

title: Human Genetic risk factors for Disseminated Coccidioidomycosis (DCM)
text: Scientific Project 3: Human Genetic Risk Factors for Disseminated Coccidioidomycosis (DCM) ABSTRACT This project will focus on elucidating human host genetic risk variants that predispose individuals to DCM. For the past 80 years, epidemiological studies have demonstrated that certain specific racial and ethnic groups were more likely to progress towards severe disseminated Coccidioidomycosis, While many of these observations have held up over, the underlying mechanistic and genetic pathogenesis underlying these epidemiological observation have not been fully evaluated. There have been several major barriers to these types of genomic studies where the relationship between host-genetic background and environment (here infection): 1) small- sample sizes for most studies; 2) challenge of handling terabytes of genomic data; 3) limited sequencing data for non-european populations;and 4) identifying relevant functional readouts to confirm the effect of variants in relevant model systems. In this U19 proposal, project 3 brings together over 600 existing exome and genome sequencing datasets and proposes to collect and sequence over 500 additional cases and controls. This will be the largest genetic study of coccidioidomycosis to date. Key to this data analysis is the experts in this proposal whose expertise enables us to handle Terabytes of data and to analyze it using ancestry-specific approaches. We will explore two major hypotheses: that common variants that make up ancestry-specific approaches underly race and ethnicity specific differences in DCM or that rare genetic variants in key immune signaling pathways increase risk of DCM. Both hypotheses are not necessarily mutually exclusive and may explain some of the disease associations that have been observed. In addition to identifying the DNA variants, we will perform ATAC-seq, RNA-sequencing studies to functionally validate non-coding and splicing changes caused by non- coding genetic variants. A key aspect of this project is its ability to rapidly integrate with projects 1 and 2 and Core C in order to validate novel genetic variants and their effects on immune pathways. It will allow us to directly bridge the gap between identified genetic variants and clinical function.

title: Gene Regulation and Physiology of Oral Streptococci
text:
Dental caries is an infectious disease that affects a large proportion of the world's population and that occurs
when the tooth is damaged by bacteria on the tooth surface that produce acids from sugars. The goal of this
research is to understand how the bacteria that cause caries coordinate the uptake and metabolism of sugars
to optimize growth and acid production. The project has high public health relevance because of the
widespread nature of dental caries, the high potential of the research to identify new opportunities for the
prevention or treatment of caries, and the applicability of the knowledge generated to a variety of other
important human pathogens.

title: Cellular Communication in Cancer Program
text: CELLULAR COMMUNICATION IN CANCER PROGRAM – PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The Cellular Communication in Cancer Program (CCC) investigates how tumor-intrinsic and systemic signaling mechanisms drive cancer initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance. Co-led by Drs. Linda Van Aelst and Corina Amor, The Program fosters research in the cross-Programmatic themes of molecular drivers of cancer, cancer heterogeneity, cancer physiology, and preclinical therapeutics and diagnostics, outlined in the CSHL-CC strategic plan, and helps with the strategic goals of fostering research in spatial biology and promoting translational research. The Program focuses on elucidating how signaling, metabolic, and neural pathways, both within tumors and across organ systems, shape cancer biology and treatment response. Notable scientific accomplishments include: 1) identification of previously unrecognized signaling vulnerabilities in pancreatic cancer and acute myeloid leukemia; 2) development of therapeutic antibodies against the PTPRD oncoprotein; 3) discovery of a novel cell death mechanism in prostate cancer; 4) elucidation of resistance pathways to metabolic therapies; 5) demonstration of immune-mediated mechanisms by which stress promotes metastasis; and 6) discovery of a hippocampal neural circuit that drives circadian disruption and immune evasion in cancer. The Program is organized around three interrelated research aims that span molecular, cellular, and systemic levels of cancer regulation. First, CCC members are defining critical signal transduction pathways that govern tumor behavior and are developing targeted therapeutic strategies that include click chemistry platforms, protein degradation technologies, biologics, and cell-based therapies. Second, the Program seeks to determine regulatory mechanisms of tumor metabolism, focusing on redox balance, lipid transport, and vitamin-related pathways. Third, CCC investigators examine how cancer is influenced at the organ and organismal level by the central and peripheral nervous systems. Ongoing interdisciplinary projects are identifying how stress, aging, circadian rhythms, and sleep shape tumor biology and immune response, and how direct interactions between tumor cells, neurons, and glial cells like microglia contribute to cancer progression. The Program includes 17 members. During the current funding cycle, CCC investigators have produced 125 publications. Of these, 29 (23%) arose from intra-Programmatic collaborations, 39 (31%) from inter-Programmatic collaborations. In addition, 65 (52%) were published in journals with an impact factor greater than 10, 101 (81%) involved collaborators at other institutions, and 57 (46%) involved collaborations with other NCI-designated cancer centers. CCC members are supported by 19 R01-equivalent grants held by 11 members. Cancer-relevant, peer- reviewed funding increased from $4M in 2020 to $5.5M in 2025, and NCI funding increased from $2.5M in 2020 to $2.9M in 2025. Collectively, CCC's integrated research efforts are uncovering fundamental mechanisms of signaling and tumor-host interactions in cancer, laying the foundation for new therapeutic strategies.

title: Mechanism and application of sugar-induced phage production by the probiotic gut symbiont Lactobacillus reuteri
text:
Our proposal is relevant to human health as we aim to understand the mechanism how diet
impacts the bacteriophage-microbe interactions, which we will exploit to promote colonization of
a probiotic, and to deliver therapeutic proteins to ameliorate diet-induced fatty liver disease.

title: Dynamic Circadian Regulation of the Blood-Brain Interface in a Human Brain-mimicking Microfluid Chip
text:
Cerebral microbleeds (CMBs), which cause blood to leak across the blood-brain interface (BBI)
and form clots within brain tissue, are pervasive in aging, dementia, and numerous other brain
disorders. CMBs are strong predictors of stroke, one of the most wide-spread and debilitating brain
disorders, whose higher incidence in the early morning and evening suggests vulnerability of the
BBI to circadian dynamics. Novel integrative approaches developed under this award to probe the
roles of circadian timing in neurovascular coagulation will contribute therapeutic strategies for
disease prevention or management, as well as promotion of health and well-being.

title: Protein Amyloid Formation and Inhibition Studied by Mass Spectrometry
text:
The formation of protein amyloid fibrils is associated with over 30 human
diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, type II diabetes, and dialysis-related
amyloidosis (DRA), but the molecular details of how these amyloids begin to form are
not well understood, which limits our ability to treat these diseases. We intend to
develop and apply new mass spectrometry based measurement tools that will yield new
molecular-level insight into the early stages of amyloid formation by β-2-microglobulin,
which is the protein associated with DRA. This new insight combined with new
approaches to screen for amyloid inhibitors will allow us to discover potential treatments
for DRA.

title: ReCARDO: Using Real-World Data to Derive Common Data Elements for Alzheimer's Disease and AD-Related Dementias Research Through Ontological Innovation
text:
We propose to create a collaborative national research network to empower and enrich NIA-funded studies
through a growing semantic-rich Real-World Data ecosystem. The resulting harmonized, validatable, cross-
sectional and longitudinal data resources will enable effective reuse of disparate and unaligned Real-World
Data to power collaborative research on Alzheimer's disease and AD-related dementias (AD/ADRD).
Ultimately, efforts from this project will accelerate the generation of new knowledge that leads to life-changing
strategies for the prevention, detection, management, and treatment of AD/ADRD.

title: Contributions of FGFR-Mediated Tumor-Stromal Interactions to Breast Cancer Growth and Progression
text:
The proposed studies focus on understanding the mechanisms through which activation of the fibroblast
growth factor (FGF) / FGF receptor (FGFR) axis drives breast cancer growth and progression. This research is
relevant to human health because understanding the mechanisms driving tumor cell-stromal interactions
during the growth and metastasis of human breast cancers will ultimately lead to the development of novel
therapeutic strategies that will improve patient outcome by enhancing initial response, preventing resistance
and reducing relapse.

title: Mining Cryptic Biosynthetic Gene Clusters for Novel Bioactive Compounds and Biocatalysts
text:
The soil-dwelling bacteria Streptomyces make numerous cyclic peptides that humans use as medicines. Analysis
of the DNA of these bacteria suggests they have the potential to make many more, but they do not make them
under standard laboratory conditions. The objectives of this proposal are to 1) computationally predict these
cyclic peptides, chemically synthesize them, and test them for interesting bioactivities and 2) to develop
biocatalysts to enable access to challenging to synthesize peptides, including strained cyclic tetrapeptides.
